newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: State power sale generates Australian dlr demand.
newsitem.headline: State power sale generates Australian dlr demand.

text.p: The Australian dollar barged higher in brisk two-way trade Monday as heavyweight U.S. bank buying overcame stubborn offers and general indifference.

Dealers harboured suspicions the demand was related to the long-rumoured A$4.5 billion purchase of a Victorian power station. "It looks like a U.S. group won the bid and is starting to take cover for their expected A$ exposure, which today has involved buying A$400 to A$500 million or so," said one.
That helped shoe-horne the currency past tough US$0.7770 resistance and trigger stop loss buying, which traders felt could carry it back to US$0.7820 offshore.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the currency had shouldered its way to US$0.7775/80, its best levels in a week, from an early US$0.7728 low and US$0.7750/55 late here Friday.

Breaking the US$0.7770 level, which had held for much of last week, was seen as a promising technical omen, although analysts emphasised that a thick layer of resistance loomed ahead at US$0.7785/95. Support now looked solid at US$0.7720 after fending off sustained selling last week.
The gains on the U.S. dollar could only partly compensate for softness on the crosses which saw it at 97.45/55 yen from 97.70/80 Friday and at 60.0 in trade weighted terms from 60.1.

The market had been anticipating the Victorian power sale for some time and speculators had even gone long of the A$ in the hope the offshore bidders would be looking to buy dollars the spot or forwards market to meet payment.

Sources close to the deal, which was Australia's largest privatisation so far, said the winning bid would be announced on Tuesday and was likely to be from a consortium led by U.S. utilities NRG Energy and CMS Energy.
Dealers are also waiting for the sale of three Federal airports to be finalised. This could fetch up to A$3.0 billion, again with a large part of the funds coming from offshore.
The prospect of such offshore demand was a welcome one for dollar bulls who had sen the currency's interest rate support steadily eroded in recent weeks.

A surprise fall in March employment data had first suggested the economy was slow to respond to the three easings delivered last year and another monetary prod might be needed. Whether such a push would be safe from an inflation point of view could well be decided by two major events this week.
The verdict on a national minimum wage claim was due Tuesday and March consumer price figures on Wednesday, and most analysts expected both to provide benign news.
The "Living Wage" claim made by Australia's main trade union body had been for an 8.75 percent increase in award wages and three annual A$20 per week pay rises for the lower paid.
The claim was savaged by the government and the Reserve Bank, with the latter estimating it could add more than 1.6 percent points to national wages growth and boost unemployment.

The RBA warned that granting the full claim could ultimately force it to tighten policy to protect its 2-3 percent target for underlying inflation. Analysts believe the threat had told with the Industrial Relations Commission, an independent body which rules on such claims, which would grant a rise of A$10-A$15.
A low outcome, say below A$12 a week, would be likely to stir speculation of a cut while a number from A$15 upwards would do much to put the talk to rest and give the A$ a filip.
The wage case could well overshadow the CPI since it was seen as the more important for gauging future inflation trends.

Nevertheless, the March quarter was expected to have seen a further slowing in price pressures with annual growth in headline CPI down to a four year low of 1.2 percent from 1.5 in Q4. The underlying rate of inflation is seen holding at 2.1 percent, the bottom of the RBA's 2-3 percent range.
